item.title: Secretary Rubio and Colombian President Abelardo De La Espriella at a Strategic Civil Nuclear Cooperation and Critical Minerals Framework Memorandums of Understanding Signing Ceremony
item.dc:creator: Marco Rubio, Secretary of State
item.description:
Marco Rubio, Secretary of State

Barranquilla, Colombia

Batallon Paraiso

Secretary Rubio and Colombian President Abelardo De La Espriella at a Strategic Civil Nuclear Cooperation and Critical Minerals Framework Memorandums of Understanding Signing Ceremony

Remarks

September 8, 2026

MODERATOR:  (Via interpreter) Good afternoon.  Good afternoon.  The Presidency of Colombia and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs would like to welcome you to the – to the ceremony of two memorandums of understanding between the Government of Colombia and the Government of the U.S. of America. 

We are pleased to have His Highness President Abelardo De La Espriella, who is the president of Colombia, that’s going to be in this act as the witness – as a witness of honor.  And we would also like to greet Omar Bula Escobar, who is the Minister of Foreign Affairs of Colombia, and His Excellency Marco Rubio, who is the Secretary of State of the United States of America, who are going to sign both agreements.

(In English) Good afternoon.  The Presidency of the Republic of Colombia and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs welcome you to the signing ceremony of two memoranda of understanding between the Government of the Republic of Colombia and the Government of the United States of America.  We are honored by the presence of His Excellency Abelardo De La Espriella, President of the Republic of Colombia, who joins us as witness of honor.  We also welcome His Excellency Omar Bula Escobar, Minister of Foreign Affairs of Colombia, and the Honorable Marco Rubio, Secretary of State of the United States of America, who will sign both instruments.

(In Spanish.)

(In English)  We will now proceed with the signing of the first memorandum of understanding, the Framework Between the Government of the United States of America and the Government of the Republic of Colombia for Securing of Supply in the Mining and Processing of Critical Minerals and Rare Earths.  (Applause.)

(The Memorandum is signed.) 

(Applause.)

(Via interpreter) Okay, thank you so much.  We will now proceed with the signing of the second memorandum of understanding that it’s called the Memorandum of Understanding Between the Government of Colombia and the United States of America about Civil Strategic Cooperation, signed by the chancellor of Colombia and the Secretary of State of the U.S.

(In English) We will now proceed with the signing of the second memorandum of understanding, the Memorandum of Understanding Between the Government of the United States of America and the Government of the Republic of Colombia Concerning Strategic Civil Nuclear Cooperation.  (Applause.)

(The Memorandum is signed.)

(Applause.)

(Via interpreter) Thank you so much.  Thank you so much.  And now we were going to go to the joint declaration about the meeting between the – the statement between Abelardo De La Espriella and the Secretary of State of the United States Marco Rubio.  And we’re going to initiate with the Secretary of State Marco Rubio.  Mr. Secretary, welcome.  Welcome. 

SECRETARY RUBIO:  (Via interpreter) Thank you so much, Mr. President.  And thank you.  I’m so glad – I’m so glad.  I came here last time as a senator but in the last four years as a senator, and then as the Secretary of State we hadn’t traveled here.  And I think that until a certain point, this is a signal of the distance that had been created between our governments, which is not natural because the relationship between Colombia and the United States is almost impossible to replicate because they are personal links, cultural links, and also – and also at the economic level.  And also we also have the opportunity to restore that natural relationships that we have between our countries, but also to grow into a new stage, a new cooperation stage with our president even stronger than we had before.

We talked a lot about security, because always security is key, because without security there is no prosperity.  But the opportunities that exist between Colombia and the U.S. is much more than security because it’s the base of everything.  Without security it’s impossible to operate as a country and as a society.  But beyond that – because sometime people say that I – now they’re telling me I’m speaking in a low – you can hear me well, right?  They say I’m speaking in a very low voice.

There is no doubt that without security a country cannot progress, and the threats to security that Colombia is facing, it’s the same things that we face in the U.S.: the same networks, the same criminal groups that, although they commit their crimes here, they also commit crimes in the U.S., and they damage our people.  But that’s the base.  That’s the key.  That’s the most relevant thing.

And because the most important role of any – of any government in any part of the world, it’s the security of its people.  But above that, we can build on prosperity, which is extremely important to move forward.  And also the opportunity that exists for Colombia at the economic level are huge, are amazing, and these are opportunities that Mr. President has in mind that we can work together so that it benefits both countries.

We have a lot to do because, unfortunately, this government inherited a series of disasters, bad decisions, and we feel – we feel the same when we went into power a year and a half ago.  But you are facing the errors of the last four years, and you need to face this.  And besides that, there was a disaster.  There was an earthquake that was tragical.

But there are amazing opportunities, and we’re going to use this opportunity that we have nowadays, because the links between our two governments are so solid to ensure that not only are we going to focus on security, but this is something going to be key in our relationship, but we’re also going to focus in what we call the opportunity of creating a prosperity that helps the North American people and also helps the Colombian people.

And this relationship between our governments have a – have direct impact on the daily life of people here but also the people in the U.S., and especially people in the certain part of Florida where I’ve lived most of my life.

If you allow, Mr. President, I’m going to give a couple of words.

(In English) I want to say a few words in English as well.  First, I want to thank the president for receiving us.  It – it’s not every day – let me say in this in Spanish first.  I should’ve said it earlier.

(Via interpreter) It’s not – and we’ve not always traveled to a country and we have the opportunity to exchange with chief of state that you met before they were president, before he was a politician, because of the mutual relationships that we have.  And even when we were talking not long ago, the two years ago when we were in the same – we were in the same table at a wedding in the southern part of Florida.  That’s why this is a place where the president of the – the president is someone that I’ve met at a personal level.  And then he went crazy and decided to become a politician and decided to turn president.

(In English) So I think that it’s unusual that you travel to a country that you meet with a head of state and a president who you’ve actually known for years before he was president, before he was even in politics.  And as I was joking, when he lost his mind and went into politics, and – but he’s going to do a great job for this country, and I know that.  I know that from what I know about him from before he was president.  This is a man of energy.  This is a man of strength.  This is a man of vision and of courage because he’s confronting a very difficult situation.  He has inherited many disasters. 

Obviously, the country faces the aftermath of a natural disaster in an earthquake, but he also faces a disaster that’s institutional, that goes through four years of very bad management and that, frankly, harmed the relationship between the United States and Colombia, something that simply is not natural.  The United States and Colombia have a strong bond that exists well beyond just the cooperation of our governments.  It’s a strong economic bond.  It’s a strong cultural bond.  It’s a strong people-to-people bond, a social bond.

I can tell you personally, having lived in south Florida the majority of my life, how we follow so closely the events that happen in Colombia, because it has a direct impact on life in south Florida and ultimately in our country.  This is the natural state of things, is for the U.S. and Colombia to be strong allies and strong partners, and the last four years is an aberration between our governments.  But that is changing as well.

Clearly, the most important obligation of any government is to provide for the security of their people.  It’s the number one obligation, and that is certainly an issue that you will confront here and that I am confident the president and his team are very serious about, and we’re going to do everything we can to help you.

But security is the basic and most important requirement of a government, but prosperity follows closely behind it, and that is opportunity of a country and an economy that provides the opportunity for upward mobility and prosperity for all of its people.  And we believe we have a lot we can do together in the field of energy, in the field of trade, in the field of commerce, that allows both countries to benefit: the people of the United States, who I work for, and the people of Colombia, who the president works for and his team works for.

So I’m excited that after not having been here for a while, to be back, to be back with someone I know so well as president, who I know has a great vision and energy for the future, and excited to be back in a country that has been our strongest ally and partner in the region for many, many years.  And we look forward not just to restoring that but building upon it and creating a golden age of relationships between our two countries and our two people.

Muchas gracias.  (Applause.)

PRESIDENT DE LA ESPRIELLA:  Thank you.

(Via interpreter) A very special welcome to all of you today.  Barranquilla has been the scenario of a – of a very strategic conversation for the present and for the future of Colombia and of our relationship with the United States of America.  To welcome the Secretary of State Marco Rubio here in the Colombian Caribbean has a very special meaning, because Barranquilla has been historically the Golden Door of Colombia to the world and represents an absolute conviction of my government because Colombia, it’s not just governed from Bogotá, Colombia; it’s governed from its regions.

I would like to thank Secretary Rubio.  His presence – we are honored by his presence.  He has been an inspiration for this battle for democracy, institutionality, and freedom because there is no Latino in the world that doesn’t feel represented by Marco Rubio, that has always done things the best way possible.  And with regards to our community, that’s why I thank you so much, Mr. Secretary of State.  It’s a pride and honor to have you here in the land of Barranquilla. 

I also would like to publicly acknowledge the solidarity of the U.S. Government after the earthquake that we endured on August 10th.  They have helped us with 26.5 million U.S. dollars in humanitarian assistance, and besides all of what they are doing regarding the fires that people are suffering near Tolima.  No country in the world has helped as much as the United States, and today we’re giving a step forward.  We are not going back from the solidarity in the emergency, to a very strategic partnership, a long-term strategic partnership. 

From this meeting there is a guideline that we’ve called the Barranquilla agreements, and they follow three main topics that are highly relevant for our country and for the hemisphere.  We are going to rebuild the homeland, we are going to recover the economy, and we are going to protect the hemisphere.  And we’re initiating a historical and close relationship that was interrupted during four years, but it has always been there in the deeper areas, in the deeper basis of Colombia, because the United States has been our partner.  We have been their ally and partner, and when the United States and Colombia have worked together, the only thing that we have had, it’s development, security, and progress. 

The main purpose of this agreement, it’s the rebuilding and the economic recovery.  The earthquake left huge challenges in households, in bridges, utilities, and in productive capacity.  We were thinking where we wanted to work on cooperation, investment, and funding mechanisms, including the – including the International Development Corporation, other agencies, the private sectors and companies from both countries.  We would like to attract investments to the infrastructure, energy, households energy, and the productive reconstruction Colombia is also going to do (inaudible) because we are going to do what we have to do regarding fiscal discipline, the legal certainty, efficiency, expanding better investment conditions.

In the same way, I requested Mr. Secretary of State to accompany us before multilateral organisms to enable instruments that allow us to fund these transitions without sacrificing the economic transition of our countries.

We are proposing to the U.S. a partnership where Colombia puts project territories, productive capabilities, resources, and clear rules and regulations (inaudible) the U.S. supports investments funding technologies and business capability. 

Other of the important points, it’s shared prosperity.  I have proposed Mr. Secretary to have this bilateral prosperity dialogue with very specific projects with – that has funding, timelines that our teams in Washington are going to continue developing.  We identified some policies regarding infrastructure, technology, industry, rebuilding, and also rare – and also rare minerals, which is the treatment we’ve just signed.  Colombia has access to two oceans, has the strategic resources and human talent.  We need to turn all those opportunities that Colombia has in investments and productive chains, in manufacturing and also in employment for our people. 

Another very important point, it’s security in the struggle against drug terrorism.  Colombia wants to become the first hemispheric security partner with the U.S., and we’re going to be the partner number one in South America.  The 21st centuries require new capabilities.  That’s why we have proposed to the government, and I said it once again today, the Patriot Plan 21st century is to update airplanes, drones, radars, helicopters, anti-drone systems, aerial defense, mobility, intelligence, cyber defense, special forces, and the maintenance and the operationality.  We’re going to have our own resource and we hope to build together capabilities to be able to face sophisticated threats.

But at the same time, we need the support – we need the support, a push from the United States, and we’re going to work in a very decisive manner in our fight against drug trafficking.  We’re going to start with – we’re going to go through the precursors, we’re going to go through the pathways, we’re going to go through the leaders, we’re going to go to the narc terrorists, we’re going to go through the money laundering and other criminal equity and also those international networks that are a huge challenge not only for the hemisphere but also for humankind.  Colombia, it’s ready to have annual quotas, verifiable indicators, and very specific agreements.  We’re going to do what we are (inaudible), and with that basis we want to have a co-responsibility that is effective for both countries.

Another important thing – it’s the Shield of Americas.  We’re already operational.  Colombia is going to fulfill its responsibilities.  We’re going to have the site in Medellín, and we’re going to do whatever it takes to be able to attack and to be able to give them the place that they deserve, which is either a prison or a tomb.  And I say it:  If a criminal doesn’t – if a criminal doesn’t follow the law, he is going to – he’s not going to get it his way.

And we also talked about Venezuela because we share more than 2,000 kilometers of borders with the neighboring countries, and everything that happens in Venezuela has a direct consequence in Colombia regarding security, migration, smuggling, armed – and armed groups, and also energy.  Colombia will participate along with the United States in a very responsible manner in the focused efforts to be able to ensure regional stability and will – and will delve on trans-border cooperation, migration, and security.  Our interest, Mr. Secretary of State, it’s that we each have institutionality, stability, and also security.  We want to avoid any type of issue.

Another very important point that I mentioned to Mr. Secretary, it’s our foreign policy is based on a main policy.  It’s that Colombia relates with the world from its own national interests.  It has sovereignty, autonomy, pragmatism, and also a long-term vision, and this is where we’re perfectly tuned with the United States.  We have now resources, geographic positions, human talent, and also very strategic assets.  Our diplomacy needs to turn those strengths in opportunities to be able to become the best partners of the U.S.  And we’re going to do it, Mr. Secretary, because this is a new rebirth.

Another very important topic, it’s migration and the rule of law.  We agreed to delve on migration – more migration cooperation, exchange of information, biometric tools, identifying of the people (inaudible) to struggle against the migrants’ networks, and also the strengthening of border controls.  Our idea, it’s that legal migration and – legal, safe, and organized migration, because our principle, it’s the same one that the United States shared.  We’re not against migration.  We’re against illegal migration, which is something different.

And there is a topic that it’s very close to my heart, and I said, Mr. Secretary, you know that many years ago we had – we had a consulate.  And I said, hey, as the son of this region, I said if you can please open a consular office in Barranquilla, the alternate capital city of Colombia.  And we are – we want a venue.  We would like to consider it if possible, Mr. Secretary, because it’s been something that we’ve expected for years.  First we had a consular office in Barranquilla, and then they took – and they removed the one from Barranquilla.  The idea, it’s to go back to things as were before, and we hope to have here in (inaudible) Barranquilla the American consular office.

And once again, a topic that it’s also close to my heart, it’s cooperation to follow the path of the money.  We would like to – we would like to see what’s money laundering resources that come from resources and hidden assets, strengthening judicial cooperation and financial cooperation. All of this, it’s going to be under the evidence of the framework of law, due process, and the respect for institutions, because to catch criminals, it’s not enough.  We also need to strike the money that supports those financial structures.  We need to affect the pocket of the criminals because it will hurt them.

This was a very deep, cordial, strategic conversation.  Not only are we talking about the United States can do for Colombia, we also talked about what Colombia and the United States can do together for the hemisphere, because Colombia contributes a geographic position, strategic resources, productive capability, human talent, a very experienced armed forces, and a government that is committed.  And we would – wanted this – this new stage to start here in Barranquilla, in the Colombian Caribbean, and in the region.  The Barranquilla agreements need to turn into projects, investments, and cooperation.

In the security and also specific outcomes, we need to rebuild the homeland.  We need to recover the economy.  We need to protect the hemisphere.  As of now, our teams (inaudible) will start to work to turn those expectations, those desires, those projects, and realities.  May God bless the United States of America.  May God bless Colombia hoy more than ever.  (Inaudible.)  Thank you.  (Applause.)

MODERATOR:  (Via interpreter) Thank you so much, Mr. President.  Thank you so much, Mr. Secretary of State.  We – in this way, we are fulfilling the agenda of Mr. Marco Rubio to the (inaudible) and city of Barranquilla.  Thank you so much.

Another important thing – it’s the Shield of Americas.  We’re already operational.  Colombia is going to fulfill its responsibilities.  We’re going to have the site in Medellín, and we’re going to do whatever it takes to be able to attack and to be able to give them the place that they deserve, which is either a prison or a tomb.  And I say it:  If a criminal doesn’t – if a criminal doesn’t follow the law, he is going to – he’s not going to get it his way.

And we also talked about Venezuela because we share more than 2,000 kilometers of borders with the neighboring countries, and everything that happens in Venezuela has a direct consequence in Colombia regarding security, migration, smuggling, armed – and armed groups, and also energy.  Colombia will participate along with the United States in a very responsible manner in the focused efforts to be able to ensure regional stability and will – and will delve on trans-border cooperation, migration, and security.  Our interest, Mr. Secretary of State, it’s that we each have institutionality, stability, and also security.  We want to avoid any type of issue.

Another very important point that I mentioned to Mr. Secretary, it’s our foreign policy is based on a main policy.  It’s that Colombia relates with the world from its own national interests.  It has sovereignty, autonomy, pragmatism, and also a long-term vision, and this is where we’re perfectly tuned with the United States.  We have now resources, geographic positions, human talent, and also very strategic assets.  Our diplomacy needs to turn those strengths in opportunities to be able to become the best partners of the U.S.  And we’re going to do it, Mr. Secretary, because this is a new rebirth.

Another very important topic, it’s migration and the rule of law.  We agreed to delve on migration – more migration cooperation, exchange of information, biometric tools, identifying of the people (inaudible) to struggle against the migrants’ networks, and also the strengthening of border controls.  Our idea, it’s that legal migration and – legal, safe, and organized migration, because our principle, it’s the same one that the United States shared.  We’re not against migration.  We’re against illegal migration, which is something different.

And there is a topic that it’s very close to my heart, and I said, Mr. Secretary, you know that many years ago we had – we had a consulate.  And I said, hey, as the son of this region, I said if you can please open a consular office in Barranquilla, the alternate capital city of Colombia.  And we are – we want a venue.  We would like to consider it if possible, Mr. Secretary, because it’s been something that we’ve expected for years.  First we had a consular office in Barranquilla, and then they took – and they removed the one from Barranquilla.  The idea, it’s to go back to things as were before, and we hope to have here in (inaudible) Barranquilla the American consular office.

And once again, a topic that it’s also close to my heart, it’s cooperation to follow the path of the money.  We would like to – we would like to see what’s money laundering resources that come from resources and hidden assets, strengthening judicial cooperation and financial cooperation. All of this, it’s going to be under the evidence of the framework of law, due process, and the respect for institutions, because to catch criminals, it’s not enough.  We also need to strike the money that supports those financial structures.  We need to affect the pocket of the criminals because it will hurt them.

This was a very deep, cordial, strategic conversation.  Not only are we talking about the United States can do for Colombia, we also talked about what Colombia and the United States can do together for the hemisphere, because Colombia contributes a geographic position, strategic resources, productive capability, human talent, a very experienced armed forces, and a government that is committed.  And we would – wanted this – this new stage to start here in Barranquilla, in the Colombian Caribbean, and in the region.  The Barranquilla agreements need to turn into projects, investments, and cooperation.

In the security and also specific outcomes, we need to rebuild the homeland.  We need to recover the economy.  We need to protect the hemisphere.  As of now, our teams (inaudible) will start to work to turn those expectations, those desires, those projects, and realities.  May God bless the United States of America.  May God bless Colombia hoy more than ever.  (Inaudible.)  Thank you.  (Applause.)

MODERATOR:  (Via interpreter) Thank you so much, Mr. President.  Thank you so much, Mr. Secretary of State.  We – in this way, we are fulfilling the agenda of Mr. Marco Rubio to the (inaudible) and city of Barranquilla.  Thank you so much.

item.title: Tajikistan Independence Day
item.dc:creator: Marco Rubio, Secretary of State
item.description:
Marco Rubio, Secretary of State

Tajikistan Independence Day

Press Statement

September 8, 2026

On behalf of the United States of America, I extend warm congratulations to the people of Tajikistan as they celebrate 35 years of independence on September 9.

The United States and Tajikistan share a strong interest in a sovereign, secure, and prosperous Central Asia. Our cooperation on border security and counterterrorism helps protect both of our countries and contributes to regional stability. Tajikistan’s hosting of the B5+1 Forum in Dushanbe will provide an important opportunity to strengthen regional economic cooperation and expand trade and investment, including opportunities for American businesses.

As Tajikistan celebrates this important anniversary, the United States remains committed to strengthening our partnership and working together to advance security and economic opportunities. We look forward to deepening the ties between our peoples and supporting greater prosperity for both of our countries.

item.title: Secretary Rubio and Colombian Foreign Minister Bula Sign Arrangements on Critical Minerals and Civil Nuclear Cooperation
item.dc:creator: Office of the Spokesperson
item.description:
Office of the Spokesperson

Secretary Rubio and Colombian Foreign Minister Bula Sign Arrangements on Critical Minerals and Civil Nuclear Cooperation

Fact Sheet

September 8, 2026

During Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s trip to Barranquilla, Colombia, on September 8, he and Colombian Foreign Minister Omar Bula signed two arrangements to advance cooperation in the fields of critical minerals and civil nuclear cooperation.  These arrangements are part of our countries’ efforts to reinvigorate the over 200-year U.S.-Colombia partnership and restore it as a linchpin of security and economic cooperation in our hemisphere.

The Critical Minerals Framework:

  • Establishes a U.S.-Colombia framework to secure resilient, diversified, and fair supply chains for critical minerals and rare earths, committing both governments to mobilize government and private sector support—via guarantees, loans, equity, offtake arrangements, insurance, or regulatory facilitation—to jointly identify and finance mining and processing projects within six months of signing.
  • Calls for streamlined permitting, market-protective pricing mechanisms such as price floors, national security review tools for critical minerals asset sales, investment in minerals recycling technology, and cooperation on geological mapping.

The Civil Nuclear Cooperation Memorandum of Understanding:

  • Establishes a bilateral framework for strategic civil nuclear cooperation between the United States and Colombia, grounded in Non-Proliferation Treaty obligations and International Atomic Energy Agency safeguards, as Colombia considers deploying nuclear power to advance energy security and deepen the two countries’ broader strategic relationship.
  • Expresses joint intent to collaborate across regulatory capacity-building, industry partnerships, and scientific and academic exchanges to support Colombia’s civil nuclear infrastructure and workforce development; explore U.S. nuclear technologies (including advanced and small modular reactors), fuel, equipment, and services; and pursue both power and non-power applications such as research reactors, radioisotopes, nuclear medicine, agriculture, and waste management—all while upholding the highest standards of safety, security, and non-proliferation.

For media inquiries, please contact the Office of the Spokesman.

item.title: Secretary of State Marco Rubio Remarks to Press
item.dc:creator: Marco Rubio, Secretary of State
item.description:
Marco Rubio, Secretary of State

Homestead, Florida

Homestead Air Reserve Base

Secretary of State Marco Rubio Remarks to Press

Remarks

September 8, 2026

SECRETARY RUBIO:  So this is an important trip, obviously.  We’re going to go visit three countries strongly aligned with the United States.  We have a lot of common interests with them, both taking on regional transnational criminal terrorism and also economic engagements.  We’re hoping to wrap up good, solid trade deals with all three of these countries in the foreseeable future.  And of course, a lot of strong cultural links.

So I think it’s part of a trend that you’re seeing in the Western Hemisphere of alignment with the U.S. and U.S. interests.  If you read our National Security Strategy – I’m sure all of you have read it very carefully page by page – it outlines one of our priorities is strengthening our presence in the Western Hemisphere.  And I think this trip and these meetings, as much as anything else, is continuing to further that goal as part of that strategy.

QUESTION:  Secretary Rubio, why not travel to Venezuela on this trip?  As you mentioned, this is all about the Western Hemisphere. 

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Well, we’ll get there eventually, as I said, but you can’t go everywhere.  This is a condensed week, obviously, with Labor Day yesterday and then 9/11 on – on Friday that we’ll be commemorating the 25th anniversary.  So we just simply couldn’t add another, and these are countries we needed to get to that I hadn’t gotten to yet.

So in the case of Colombia, they just had a free and democratic election.  They elected someone I know very well, very aligned with the U.S., and we want to – we have a longstanding relationship.  In the case of Peru, after some political turmoil, they too have had a recent election, and President Fujimori is someone we look forward to engaging with.  And then in Ecuador, obviously, their election was last year but they face – they’re one of our closest security partners in the region, and I think there’s more we can do with them – economics as well.

QUESTION:  Secretary Rubio, what would your message be to Latin Americans who might look at the Venezuela oil deal and think that the U.S. Government’s interested in extracting resources or just sending troops?

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Well, I —

QUESTION:  What’s your message?

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Well, what I would say to anyone who is concerned that the U.S. is doing something negative towards the Western Hemisphere as regards to energy is those oil fields, once dominated by China and Russia and Iran, by the way; Iran also had some concessions – and they’re no longer there.  So I think they’re much better off partnering with the United States.  They will benefit greatly from it.  These fields were in many cases nonproductive; in essence, the Chinese and Russian companies held these fields but never turned them into anything.  These fields are going to be productive and they’re going to generate royalties and revenues for the Venezuelan people – eventually through a democratically elected government, hopefully sooner rather than later – and directly benefit the people of Venezuela, as opposed to going into the pocket of some corrupt government official or in the hands of American and Venezuelan adversaries, really.

QUESTION:  Mr. Secretary, do you have anything to say about the British decision on the imports from Israel – or from settlements in —

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Well, they alerted us to it.  We don’t have any announcements.  Obviously, these are decisions that they make.  And we and the President has expressed this in the past:  We don’t want to see anything destabilizing going on right now in the West Bank with so much going on in the region.  We think it has implications as well on our ability to make progress with regards to Gaza and the 20-point plan and Board of Peace that we’re very committed to.  Obviously, we’re not going to do what the UK did.  We saw their announcement today, but I don’t have any comment on it right now.

QUESTION:  But Ambassador Huckabee said that you’ve – that the Brits will suffer because of that with the U.S., that he suggested that the U.S. —

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Well, I would say that the President has not commented on this.  As I said, neither have I at this point.  We were made aware that they were going to make this decision.  We heard their arguments as to why.  But look, we share the goal of stability.  We don’t want to see some uptick in violence or an uptick in conflict or tensions in the West Bank at a very tenuous time in the region.  There’s always tenuous times.  But beyond that, I don’t think – as of this moment, we don’t have any further comment on the UK decision that I think was announced just a few hours ago. 

QUESTION:  Overnight the Houthis launched a substantial attack on Saudi Arabia.  What are your thoughts on that when the U.S. has put pressure on the Houthis to kind of stay out of this fight?

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Yeah, look, again, the Houthis in many ways are agents and proxies of the Iranians.  I think behind some of this is clearly the Iranian hand.  The U.S. has a very strong defensive military relationship with Saudi Arabia, and we’re watching those events very closely.  It’s been going on for some time.  I think there’s been some ground operations as well where many forces are taking on the Houthis and pushing back against some of the ground advances that they attempted to make.  And we’re monitoring that, as I said, very, very closely.  And – but I would defer as far as on the defense side to the Department of War.  I don’t think there’ll be any announcements on that today.

item.title: Operation Economic Outcast Grounds Iran’s Aviation Sector
item.dc:creator: Thomas "Tommy" Pigott, SpokesmanOffice of the Spokesperson
item.description:
Thomas "Tommy" Pigott, SpokesmanOffice of the Spokesperson

Operation Economic Outcast Grounds Iran’s Aviation Sector

Press Statement

September 8, 2026

Today, the United States continues implementation of Operation Economic Outcast by sanctioning 36 entities and individuals in multiple jurisdictions for aiding Iran’s aviation sector. This sector has enabled the regime to support proliferation and terrorism worldwide.

On August 24, 2026, the U.S. Department of the Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) determined that Executive Order (E.O.) 13902 shall apply to Iran’s aviation sector, among others.  Under that authority, OFAC is designating the remainder of Iran’s active airlines, furthering our campaign to isolate the Iranian regime from the international system and global economy.  Today, OFAC is also targeting several third country‑based firms that have provided cargo and general sales services to, and procured aircraft for, Iran’s largest airline, Mahan Air, which has been designated in connection to the regime’s proliferation and terrorism-support activities around the world.

We will not relent in our campaign to shut down the Iranian regime’s financial lifelines, including the aviation sector. 

Today’s actions are being taken pursuant to E.O. 13224, as amended, a counterterrorism authority, and E.O. 13902, which targets certain sectors of the Iranian economy. On October 12, 2011, OFAC designated Mahan Air pursuant to E.O. 13224 for providing financial, material, and technological support to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps-Quds Force (IRGC-QF), which OFAC designated pursuant to E.O. 13224 in October 2007 for providing support to multiple terrorist organizations.  On December 11, 2019, the U.S. Department of State designated Mahan Air pursuant to E.O. 13382, which targets weapons of mass destruction (WMD) proliferators and their supporters. For more information on today’s action, please see the Department of the Treasury’s Press Release.

item.title: Andorra National Day
item.dc:creator: Marco Rubio, Secretary of State
item.description:
Marco Rubio, Secretary of State

Andorra National Day

Press Statement

September 8, 2026

On behalf of the United States of America, I extend warm wishes to the people of Andorra as they celebrate their patron saint, Our Lady of Meritxell.

The United States values Andorra as a steadfast friend that shares our commitment to national sovereignty and a secure, prosperous future for its citizens. The United States is proud of the momentum built over the past year in our relationship with the Principality of Andorra, particularly Andorra’s continued collaboration with American technology companies to strengthen its digital infrastructure and financial sector security. We look forward to building on this foundation in the coming year, expanding opportunities for U.S. businesses and investment.

As the people of Andorra celebrate this important day, the United States reaffirms its partnership with the Principality and extends our warmest regards to the Andorran people in the year ahead.

item.title: U.S. Sanctions Dismantle the Iranian Regime’s Revenue Streams
item.dc:creator: Thomas "Tommy" Pigott, SpokesmanOffice of the Spokesperson
item.description:
Thomas "Tommy" Pigott, SpokesmanOffice of the Spokesperson

U.S. Sanctions Dismantle the Iranian Regime’s Revenue Streams

Press Statement

September 4, 2026

The United States remains committed to cutting off the Iranian regime’s access to the international financial system and the resources it uses to destabilize the region and threaten U.S. interests and partners. Today’s U.S. Department of the Treasury sanctions on Türkiye-based Golden Global Bank mark the latest step in Operation Economic Outcast, a whole-of-government effort to sever the networks that allow the regime to launder funds, evade sanctions, and finance its terrorist proxies across the Middle East.

This action sends a clear message to financial institutions worldwide: facilitating Iran’s illicit financial activity carries serious consequences. This demonstrates the Trump Administration’s commitment to eliminating resources the regime uses to threaten regional stability, support terrorism, and advance its military capabilities.

The United States will continue to use every diplomatic and economic tool at its disposal to isolate the Iranian regime until it abandons its support for terrorism and its destabilizing activities in the region. We urge the international community to join this effort and ensure no institution serves as a financial lifeline for a regime that threatens peace and security.

Today’s action is being taken pursuant to Executive Order (E.O.) 13902, which targets the financial sector of Iran’s economy and advances Operation Economic Outcast—a campaign to completely isolate the regime from the financial lifelines that sustain its malign behavior. Please see the Department of the Treasury’s Press Release.

item.title: Secretary Rubio’s Travel to Colombia, Ecuador, and Peru
item.dc:creator: Thomas "Tommy" Pigott, SpokesmanOffice of the Spokesperson
item.description:
Thomas "Tommy" Pigott, SpokesmanOffice of the Spokesperson

Secretary Rubio’s Travel to Colombia, Ecuador, and Peru

Press Statement

September 4, 2026

Secretary of State Marco Rubio will travel to Colombia, Ecuador, and Peru from September 8-10 to strengthen key U.S. partnerships in our region. During the trip, he will meet with the new De La Espriella government in Colombia, President Noboa in Ecuador, and the new Fujimori government in Peru to discuss U.S. support for Colombia’s earthquake response; enhanced cooperation in the shared fight against narcoterrorism, which threatens our hemisphere; and the benefits of deeper commercial relationships between our countries.

Throughout the trip, the Secretary will reaffirm the Trump Administration’s commitment to a secure, prosperous, and democratic Western Hemisphere.

item.title: Quad Sherpas’ Meeting in New Delhi
item.dc:creator: Office of the Spokesperson
item.description:
Office of the Spokesperson

Quad Sherpas’ Meeting in New Delhi

Media Note

September 3, 2026

India’s Foreign Secretary Shri Vikram Misri hosted a Quad Sherpas’ Meeting in New Delhi on September 3, 2026. The meeting was attended by Ms. Elly Lawson, Deputy Secretary, Strategic Planning & Coordination Group, Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade, Australia; Mr. Hiroyuki Namazu, Senior Deputy Minister for Foreign Affairs, Japan; and Mr. Sergio Gor, Special Envoy to South and Central Asia and Ambassador of USA to India.

The Quad Sherpas’ Meeting follows the Quad Foreign Ministers’ Meeting held in New Delhi on May 26, 2026 and was convened to take forward its outcomes and to prepare for the next Quad Foreign Ministers’ Meeting.

The Sherpas reviewed progress across ongoing Quad initiatives and discussed ways to further strengthen practical cooperation, with a shared commitment to advancing a free and open Indo-Pacific.

Discussions covered key areas of Quad cooperation, including maritime and transnational security; economic prosperity and security; critical and emerging technologies; and humanitarian assistance and emergency response. The Sherpas also exchanged views on developments in the Indo-Pacific and the broader regional and global context.

The Quad Sherpas reaffirmed the importance of focusing on concrete, action-oriented initiatives. They looked forward to continued consultations in the lead-up to the next Quad Foreign Ministers’ Meeting.
